"title": "Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440",
"authors": "Paul M. Harvey and Andrew Oldag",
"field_subfield": "Astronomy: circumstellar mass loss and dust shells around AGB stars",
"type_of_paper": "Observational + modeling study (single lunar occultation event)",
"executive_summary": "Harvey & Oldag (2007) present the first multi-spectral lunar occultation observations of the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440, obtained with the high-speed infrared spectrophotometer pMIRAS on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope during an immersion event on 28 Aug 2001. The observations spanned a continuous wavelength range of 1–4µm with a time resolution of 8 msec, enabling milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The authors found that the occultation fringes could not be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observations simultaneously probe the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. They used the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell, fitting both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yielded a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K, and an optical depth at 5µm of 0.5 ± 0.1. The density gradient was best described by ρ ∝ r−2 or the gradient derived by Ivezić & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The authors also derived a dust mass-loss rate of 6.5 × 10−8 M⊙/yr, consistent with prior estimates. A notable tension emerged: the models could not fit the observed IRAS 60µm flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate. This work resolved the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the dust shell separately, providing strong constraints on the inner dust shell structure. The findings support radiatively driven mass loss but reveal a discrepancy at far-infrared wavelengths that may reflect non-constant outflow. The study highlights the power of lunar occultations for high-angular-resolution diagnostics of circumstellar environments.",

summary.title: Multi-spectral Observations of Lunar Occultations: I. Resolving The Dust Shell Around AFGL 5440
summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey and Andrew Oldag
summary.field_subfield: Astronomy: circumstellar mass loss and dust shells around AGB stars
summary.type_of_paper: Observational + modeling study (single lunar occultation event)
summary.executive_summary: Harvey & Oldag (2007) present the first multi-spectral lunar occultation observations of the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440, obtained with the high-speed infrared spectrophotometer pMIRAS on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope during an immersion event on 28 Aug 2001. The observations spanned a continuous wavelength range of 1–4µm with a time resolution of 8 msec, enabling milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The authors found that the occultation fringes could not be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observations simultaneously probe the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. They used the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell, fitting both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yielded a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K, and an optical depth at 5µm of 0.5 ± 0.1. The density gradient was best described by ρ ∝ r−2 or the gradient derived by Ivezić & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The authors also derived a dust mass-loss rate of 6.5 × 10−8 M⊙/yr, consistent with prior estimates. A notable tension emerged: the models could not fit the observed IRAS 60µm flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate. This work resolved the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the dust shell separately, providing strong constraints on the inner dust shell structure. The findings support radiatively driven mass loss but reveal a discrepancy at far-infrared wavelengths that may reflect non-constant outflow. The study highlights the power of lunar occultations for high-angular-resolution diagnostics of circumstellar environments.

claims.description: Lunar occultations with high-speed spectrophotometry can resolve the inner dust shell structure of carbon-rich AGB stars.
The maximum dust temperature near 950 K is a strong constraint on the inner dust shell location.
The IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit without graphite or higher past mass loss, indicating a possible recent decrease in mass-loss rate.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Harvey & Oldag (2007) present the first multi-spectral lunar occultation observations of the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440, obtained with the high-speed infrared spectrophotometer pMIRAS on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope during an immersion event on 28 Aug 2001. The observations spanned a continuous wavelength range of 1–4µm with a time resolution of 8 msec, enabling milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The authors found that the occultation fringes could not be fit by any single-size model, indicating that the observations simultaneously probe the central star and a circumstellar dust shell produced by stellar mass loss. They used the DUSTY radiative transfer code to model a circumstellar shell, fitting both the observed occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution (SED) from the literature. The best-fitting models yielded a strong constraint on the inner radius of the dust shell, with a maximum dust temperature of Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K, and an optical depth at 5µm of 0.5 ± 0.1. The density gradient was best described by ρ ∝ r−2 or the gradient derived by Ivezić & Elitzur for a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. The authors also derived a dust mass-loss rate of 6.5 × 10−8 M⊙/yr, consistent with prior estimates. A notable tension emerged: the models could not fit the observed IRAS 60µm flux without assuming a substantial abundance of graphite or a substantially higher past mass-loss rate. This work resolved the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the dust shell separately, providing strong constraints on the inner dust shell structure. The findings support radiatively driven mass loss but reveal a discrepancy at far-infrared wavelengths that may reflect non-constant outflow. The study highlights the power of lunar occultations for high-angular-resolution diagnostics of circumstellar environments.

Research Context
Mass loss from post-main-sequence stars supplies heavy elements and solids to the ISM. AGB mass loss involves radiation pressure and stellar pulsation, but details are poorly understood. Molecular line studies reveal periodic mass-loss variations producing 'rings' in radial distributions. Deep imaging has found similar phenomena in dust around IRC+10216. Studying inner circumstellar shells requires angular resolutions well under 1 arcsec. Most interferometric observations have used only one or two broad bands. Lunar occultations and multi-aperture interferometry reach milli-arcsecond resolutions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
What is the spatial structure of the circumstellar dust shell around AFGL 5440? Can a single-size model fit the occultation fringes, or is a shell required? What are the inner radius, temperature, and density gradient of the dust shell? What dust composition fits the SED, including the IRAS 60µm flux? Can the IRAS 60µm flux be fit without graphite or higher past mass loss? What dust mass-loss rate is implied by the optical depth and density gradient?

Methodological Details
The study observed the carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440 (aka OH 06.86-1.5, IRAS 18036-2344). Observations were made during an immersion occultation event on 28 Aug 2001 at approximately 02:44:00 UT. The Moon elevation was 36°, the Sun 17° below the horizon, position angle 54°, and lunar phase 0.72. Observations used the pMIRAS instrument on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The instrument is a long/wide slit, high-speed spectrophotometer using a NaCl prism. Light was imaged onto a 32×100 pixel portion of a 256² InSb array detector. The slit width was set at about 5 arcsec for typical seeing of 1.5 arcsec. The detector was read-out every 8 msec with photon integration over essentially the full 8 msec. Observations covered 1–4µm with resolving power from ~20 at short wavelengths to ~100 at long wavelengths. On average, one pixel corresponds to λ/∆λ = 100. The plate scale in the spatial direction was 0.4 arcsec/pixel. The instrument is read-noise limited shortward of 2.5µm and background-limited longward of 3µm.

Procedures And Architectures
A typical observation consisted of taking 5000 frames centered on the occultation event. The buffer holds the most recent 5000 frames to accommodate errors in predicted event times. Predicted occultation times can be in error by up to 10 seconds due to lunar limb irregularities. The data reduction shifts images to the same wavelength/pixel scale via cross-correlation. Detector tilt relative to X/Y axes was removed during processing. Sky subtraction used sky measurements on either side of the stellar spectrum. The reduction produced a weighted average two pixels wide in the spectral direction. The end result was a sequence of ~100 light curves with a few hundred frames each. Wavelength calibration fit the NaCl dispersion function to J, H, K, and L atmospheric transmission maxima. The calibration accuracy was good to ±0.01λ throughout the 1–4µm region. No flux calibration was attempted due to variable efficiency and non-photometric conditions. Relative signal was compared to well-characterized stars, consistent with literature magnitudes within ±30%.

Key Results
A single-size uniform disk model could not fit the AFGL 5440 fringes across 1–4µm. An 11 mas uniform disk fit mid-range wavelengths (2.5–3.2µm) but failed at short and long wavelengths. The maximum dust temperature was constrained to Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K. Models with Tmax below 900 K lacked hot dust to fit long-wavelength fringes. The radial density gradient was close to r−2 or the Ivezić & Elitzur radiatively driven wind gradient. The optical depth at 5µm was 0.5 ± 0.1 for the best-fitting model. The best dust composition included SiC with comparable amounts of amorphous carbon and graphite. The dust mass-loss rate was 6.5 × 10−8 M⊙/yr for DUSTY amorphous carbon optical constants. The inner dust shell radius was 3.7×10¹⁴ cm, or 11 mas at 2.25 kpc. The central star angular diameter was of order 3 mas at 2500 K ± 300 K. The dust emissivity was ε ∝ λ−1.3, consistent with amorphous carbon-rich dust. Groenewegen et al. derived a gas mass-loss rate of 3.1×10−5 M⊙/yr and dust mass-loss rate of 5.1×10−8 M⊙/yr.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The observations resolved the stellar photosphere and the inner edge of the dust shell separately. The inner dust shell temperature near 950 K constrains the inner radius location. The inner radius is nearly a factor of two below expected dust condensation temperatures. The density gradient is consistent with radiatively driven mass loss. The dust mass-loss rate is consistent with prior estimates of 5–10×10−8 M⊙/yr. The inability to fit the IRAS 60µm flux without graphite is a strong constraint. The 60µm discrepancy may imply a recent decrease in mass-loss rate. This contrasts with Suh (1997), who proposed higher recent mass-loss rates.

Contradictions And Limitations
No flux calibration was attempted due to variable efficiency and non-photometric conditions. The ±30% uncertainty in stellar magnitudes limits absolute flux comparisons. The data were limited to accuracies on the order of ±2 mas. A discrepancy near 1.7µm for IRC+00233 remains unexplained. The IRAS 60µm flux could not be fit without graphite or higher past mass loss. The graphite requirement contradicts evidence against graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. The dust composition range for amorphous carbon was not fully explored. The stellar photosphere details were not thoroughly examined. The IRAS LRS agreement was only superficial. The 60µm discrepancy explanation is beyond the scope of the study.

Claims
Lunar occultations with high-speed spectrophotometry can resolve the inner dust shell structure of carbon-rich AGB stars. The observations achieved milli-arcsecond angular resolution. The occultation fringes were fit by a circumstellar shell model. The inner dust shell radius was constrained to 11 mas. The IRAS 60µm flux could not be fit without graphite. The graphite requirement contradicts prior evidence. The method constrains the dust density gradient and mass-loss rate. The technique can be applied to other carbon-rich AGB stars.
The maximum dust temperature near 950 K is a strong constraint on the inner dust shell location. The best-fitting models had Tmax = 950 K ± 50 K. Models below 900 K lacked hot dust to fit long-wavelength fringes. The inner radius is nearly a factor of two below condensation temperatures. Ivezić & Elitzur (1996) derived a lower inner dust shell temperature of ~750 K. The temperature constraint defines the inner edge of the dust shell. The result supports radiatively driven mass loss.
The IRAS 60µm flux cannot be fit without graphite or higher past mass loss, indicating a possible recent decrease in mass-loss rate. Models with only amorphous carbon and SiC failed to fit the 60µm flux by factors of 3 or more. The 60µm discrepancy may imply a recent decrease in mass-loss rate. The radial location of 60µm dust is 1 to a few arcseconds from the star. This contrasts with Suh (1997), who proposed higher recent mass-loss rates. The 60µm discrepancy may reflect non-constant outflow. The time scale is comparable to the IRC+10216 fluctuation period.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study explored more than 200 models to understand parameter effects. Models with r−1.8 came closer to the IRAS 60µm flux but fit the 5–20µm SED poorly. Models with r−2.2 fit the SED out to 20µm but had worse IRAS 60µm fits. The outer radius makes no difference at λ < 60µm if at least 100 times the inner radius. Both MRN and KMH grain size distributions produced reasonable fits. A model without graphite fit the SED but gave a poor occultation fit.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows observed and model light curves for a 4.5 mas uniform disk model. Figure 2 shows χ² and signal-to-noise ratio as a function of wavelength. Figures 3 and 4 show HD 155292 uniform-disk fits with sizes less than 3 mas. Figure 5 shows AFGL 5440 light curves indicating a single size is unlikely to fit. Figures 7 and 8 show the best-fitting model fits to the SED and occultation light curves. Figure 9 shows the quality of the fit versus wavelength. Figure 10 illustrates the spatial profiles of the best-fitting model. Figures 11 and 12 show the best-fitting model without graphite. Figures 13 and 14 show a model that fits the SED but poorly fits the occultation.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: First multi-spectral lunar occultation observations of AFGL 5440 resolved the inner dust shell structure. 2. The strongest evidence: The maximum dust temperature of 950 K ± 50 K and density gradient of r−2 strongly constrain the inner dust shell. 3. The future path: The IRAS 60µm discrepancy may require graphite or non-constant outflow, pointing to further study of mass-loss variations.
